div.p: Researchers commonly use analysis of variance (ANOVA) to statistically test results of factorial designs. Performing an a-priori power analysis is crucial to ensure that the ANOVA is sufficiently powered, however, it often poses a challenge and can result in large sample sizes, especially if the expected effect size is small. Due to the high prevalence of small effect sizes in psychology, studies are frequently underpowered as it is often economically unfeasible to gather the necessary sample size for adequate Type II error control. Here, we present a more efficient alternative to the fixed ANOVA, the so-called sequential ANOVA that we implemented in the R package "sprtt". The sequential ANOVA is based on the sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) that uses a likelihood ratio as a test statistic and controls for long-term error rates. SPRTs gather evidence for both the null and the alternative hypothesis and conclude this process when a sufficient amount of evidence has been gathered to accept one of the two hypotheses. Through simulations, we show that the sequential ANOVA is more efficient than the fixed ANOVA and reliably controls long-term error rates. Additionally, robustness analyses revealed that the sequential and fixed ANOVA exhibit analogous properties when their underlying assumptions are violated. Taken together, our results demonstrate that the sequential ANOVA is an efficient alternative to fixed sample designs for hypothesis testing.

div.head: Sequential Analysis of Variance: Increasing Efficiency of Hypothesis Testing
div.p: When testing hypotheses, fixed-sample designs such as the Neyman-Pearson procedure (Neyman & Pearson, 1933) are the method of choice in psychological research.

The Neyman-Pearson procedure allows researchers to decide between two competing statistical hypotheses with certain probabilities to make an erroneous decision. These probabilities are denoted by 𝛼, the probability to falsely reject a true null hypothesis 𝐻 0 (Type-I error), and 𝛽, the probability to falsely reject a true alternative hypothesis 𝐻 1 (Type-II error). While the former is controlled by choosing an appropriate critical value for the test statistic, the latter is controlled by collecting a sufficiently large sample size, which is determined by an a priori power analysis (Cohen, 1992;Erdfelder et al., 1996).

Even though this procedure is widely accepted as a nominal standard in psychology, a priori power analyses are not without challenges. First, researchers must specify an expected effect size, which may be difficult. If neither a precise prediction nor previously reported effect sizes are available to guide the specification, a reasonable approach is to use the smallest effect size of interest (Lakens, 2022). This strategy, however, is related to a second challenge: The required sample size for a statistical test is a function of the test procedure (e.g., parametric vs. non-parametric tests), the desired 𝛼 (which is usually set to .05 or lower), the statistical power 1 -𝛽 (which is usually set to .80 or higher), and the hypotheses, that is, the expected effect size. When the effect size is small, the sample size required to ensure sufficiently low error probabilities is large. Unfortunately, psychological effects are typically small or medium sized (Funder & Ozer, 2019;Richard et al., 2003;Roberts et al., 2007). Thus, power analyses based on realistic effect-size expectations or smallest effect sizes of interest typically yield required sample sizes that exceed available resources. As a result, psychological studies are often based on too small sample sizes and thus underpowered (Button et al., 2013;Rossi, 1990;Szucs & Ioannidis, 2017).

A promising way to overcome the pervasive problem of underpowered studies due to scarce resources is to resort to more efficient statistical testing procedures, namely, sequential hypothesis tests. Almost 80 years ago, Abraham Wald devised a sequential procedure to increase the efficiency of statistical decision-making in industrial production, the sequential probability ratio test (SPRT; Wald, 1945). Despite their favorable properties, the SPRT and other sequential designs have long been neglected in psychological research.

Fostered by the increasing awareness of the need for efficient hypothesis-testing procedures and recent publications on the topic (e.g., Lakens, 2014;Pramanik et al., 2021;Schnuerch & Erdfelder, 2020;Schönbrodt et al., 2017;Stefan et al., 2022), however, there is a growing interest in sequential designs. With this article, we further support this development by implementing an SPRT for one of the most common test procedures, namely, the one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). By thoroughly testing this sequential ANOVA in comparison to the conventional fixed-sample approach and by implementing it in a user-friendly R package, we hope to make the SPRT and sequential testing in general more accessible as a useful tool for psychological researchers in all subfields.

div.head: The Sequential Probality Ratio Test
div.p: Like the seminal theory of statistical decision making by Neyman and Pearson (Neyman & Pearson, 1933), the SPRT is a procedure for testing statistical hypotheses with controlled error probabilities (Wald, 1945;Wald, 1947). Unlike classical test procedures, however, the SPRT dispenses with the requirement of a fixed sample size (Wald, 1945).

Instead, a decision is made after each observation whether the data collection can be terminated or needs to be continued. This flexibility to terminate early when there is compelling evidence in the data for one or the other hypothesis leads to an attractive feature: Compared to a fixed-sample design with the same error probabilities, the SPRT requires on average up to 50% smaller sample sizes (Schnuerch & Erdfelder, 2020;Wald, 1945). Thus, it is a highly efficient alternative to conventional testing procedures that control statistical decision errors.

The basic principle of the SPRT can be described as follows. The data are collected and monitored continuously. After each additional observation, a decision is made based on a predefined decision criterion whether one of the specified hypotheses (𝐻 0 or 𝐻 1 ) can be accepted, in which case sampling is terminated. Otherwise, the data collection must be continued. Thus, the final sample size is a random variable that depends on the sequence of collected observations and the specified decision criterion.

Let us assume that we are interested in the random variable X, with 𝑋 ∼ 𝑓(𝑥; 𝜃), where 𝜃 denotes the true but unknown parameter vector of the underlying population and 𝑓(.) may be either a probability mass function (if 𝑋 is discrete) or a probability density function (if 𝑋 is continuous). Further assume that we wish to test the two competing hypotheses 𝐻 0 : 𝜃 = 𝜃 0 versus 𝐻 1 : 𝜃 = 𝜃 1 . The central component of the SPRT is the ratio of probabilities of the oberved data under the two hypotheses, that is, the likelihood ratio (𝐿𝑅). The 𝐿𝑅 is a measure of relative statistical evidence in the data for the specified hypotheses (Etz, 2018). Importantly, this interpretation is independent of how the data were sampled (Rouder, 2014). Starting at 𝑛 = 1, the 𝐿𝑅 is calculated after any 𝑛th observation. Let x (𝑛) = (𝑥 1 , … , 𝑥 𝑛 ) be the vector of data at the 𝑛th stage. The 𝐿𝑅 at this stage is given by 𝐿𝑅 𝑛 = 𝑓(x (𝑛) ; 𝜃 1 ) 𝑓(x (𝑛) ; 𝜃 0 ) .

Data collection continues by adding independent observations 𝑥 𝑛+1 as long as 𝐵 < 𝐿𝑅 𝑛 < 𝐴, where 𝐴 and 𝐵 denote predefined constants with 𝐵 < 𝐴. As soon as 𝐿𝑅 𝑛 ≥ 𝐴, sampling is terminated and 𝐻 0 is rejected (𝐻 1 is accepted); if, in contrast, 𝐿𝑅 𝑛 ≤ 𝐵, sampling is terminated and 𝐻 0 is accepted (𝐻 1 is rejected). Even though the exact sample size is unknown beforehand, it was shown that this sequential procedure terminates with a probability of one after a finite number of observations (Wald, 1945).

To ensure that the test satisfies error probabilities 𝛼 and 𝛽 under 𝐻 0 and 𝐻 1 , respectively, appropriate values for 𝐴 and 𝐵 must be chosen. In practical applications, the choice is surprisingly simple: Wald (1945) showed that in order to achieve the desired error probabilities, upper and lower limits for 𝐴 and 𝐵 are given by (1 -𝛽)/𝛼 and 𝛽/(1 -𝛼), respectively. The SPRT controls statistical decision errors in the same way as conventional test procedures with fixed sample sizes. In addition, it has the advantage of stopping early when there is compelling evidence in the data. In fact, Wald and Wolfowitz (1948) proved that the SPRT has an optimum property, that is, for given hypotheses and error rates, there is no (sequential or non-sequential) test procedure that requires a smaller sample size on average than the SPRT. This proof, however, only holds for simple hypotheses. A hypothesis is considered simple if the probability distribution is fully specified, that is, all parameters of the statistical model are either known or defined by the hypothesis. If, in contrast, there is at least one free parameter, the hypothesis is composite (Neyman & Pearson, 1933). For example, when testing hypotheses about the mean of a normally distributed variable with unknown population variance 𝜎 2 , the hypotheses are composite as long as they do not specify the value of 𝜎 2 . In psychological research, population variances are typically unknown, which limits the applicability of the original SPRT as outlined above. However, extensions of the SPRT have solved this issue for a range of testing scenarios, for example, sequential 𝑡-tests (Hajnal, 1961;Rushton, 1950). Even though the proof of the SPRT's optimum property does not necessarily hold for these scenarios, the sequential tests have been shown to still be much more efficient than corresponding fixed-sample tests (e.g., Schnuerch & Erdfelder, 2020).

Despite their efficiency and flexibility, SPRTs are not very popular in psychology (Ulrich & Miller, 2021). One of the reasons for the widespread neglect of sequential procedures may be that, first, most of the current literature on the SPRT focuses on t-tests and not on more complex applications (e.g., Schnuerch & Erdfelder, 2020;Stefan et al., 2022; but see Schnuerch et al., 2020Schnuerch et al., , 2022)). Second, SPRTs exist mainly in the literature but not in easily applicable, well-documented, and flexible statistics software (Albers, 2019).

In order to address the first problem and improve the applicability of SPRTs, we implemented a sequential one-way fixed-effects ANOVA that allows researchers to perform efficient hypothesis tests on multiple means instead of only two. In the present study, we investigate through simulations its properties in direct comparison to a fixed-sample ANOVA and demonstrate that the sequential ANOVA controls 𝛼 and 𝛽 notably more efficiently. We also report the procedures' performances under imperfect conditions such as unequal sample sizes or violations of homoscedasticity. Finally, we illustrate and discuss a limitation of sequential ANOVAs, namely, biased effect-size estimation following a sequential test.

In order to address the second problem, we developed the sprtt (Sequential Probability Ratio Test Toolbox) package in R, which contains implementations of the sequential ANOVA and sequential t-tests (Steinhilber et al., 2023). The package was published on CRAN and the latest development version can be found on GitHub: https://github.com/MeikeSteinhilber/sprtt. The implementation was done carefully in consideration of future extendability and maintenance requirements. This user-friendly package makes applications of the SPRT straightforward and convenient for applied researchers. We hope that addressing these two issues -implementing a sequential one-way fixed-effects ANOVA and making SPRTs easily available in an R package -will contribute to the growing popularity of sequential analysis in psychological research.

div.head: Alternative Sequential Designs
div.p: A sequential procedure that is closely related to the SPRT is the so-called Sequential Bayes Factor Test (SBFT; Schönbrodt et al., 2017). The SBFT uses Bayes factors instead of likelihood ratios as a test statistic. To calculate Bayes factors, prior distributions are defined for unknown parameters and the likelihood is then integrated (marginalized) across these priors (Morey & Rouder, 2011;Wagenmakers et al., 2010).

Thus, the Bayes factor can be understood as a weighted average of likelihoods with priors as weights (Rouder et al., 2009). Using a prior distribution instead of a point hypothesis has the advantage that researchers do not have to commit to a single effect size but that they can specify a range of plausible values. As has been shown in the context of sequential 𝑡-tests, this can decrease the efficiency especially for small to medium effect sizes, but it increases the robustness against model misspecifications (i.e., when the true effect size differs from the expected effect size; see Schnuerch & Erdfelder, 2020;Stefan et al., 2022).

In contrast, SPRTs are on average more efficient and allow for the explicit control of error rates, but they are more sensitive to model misspecifications (Schnuerch & Erdfelder, 2020;Stefan et al., 2022). In the end, both methods are very similar and the decision to use either an SPRT with point hypotheses or an SBFT with prior distributions likely reflects a general preference for one statistical theory (i.e., frequentism vs. Bayesianism) over the other. As has recently been shown, the two procedures can even be integrated to combine the benefits of both into a single testing framework (Schnuerch et al., 2022).

Other sequential procedures such as the Group Sequential Design (GSD; Lang, 2017;Proschan et al., 2006) or the Independent Segments Procedure (ISP; Miller & Ulrich, 2021) differ conceptually more from SPRTs than the SBFT. SPRTs allow for termination after any single observation while the final sample size is unknown beforehand (i.e., it is a non-truncated procedure). The ISP, in contrast, uses a priori planned interim analyses of batches of observations up to a precisely defined maximum (i.e., a truncated procedure).
This sampling plan allows the analyst to stop data collection only at these planned stops.

Although the ISP is more efficient than corresponding fixed-sample designs, due to this reduced flexibility in the sampling plan, it is on average less efficient compared to SPRTs (Erdfelder & Schnuerch, 2021).

GSDs are a family of test designs that allow for interim analyses (looks) and early termination based on different approaches to control error probabilities that vary in their complexity and flexibility (Lakens et al., 2021). Simpler but also less flexible versions use procedures such as the Pocock or O'Brien and Fleming procedure to correct the critical values for early stopping at each look (Lakens et al., 2021;O'Brien & Fleming, 1979;Pocock, 1977). However, these corrections can only be used if the number of looks as well as the required sample size for each look is known beforehand. More flexible alternatives use so-called spending functions that allow the analyst to control how the 𝛼 and 𝛽 rates are spent across looks while the exact number of looks and sample sizes are not required to be specified in advance (Lakens et al., 2021;Lan & DeMets, 1983).

One of the main advantages of GSDs and the ISP over non-truncated designs such as the SPRT is that 𝑁 max is known beforehand, which may be important for researchers when planning a study (Miller & Ulrich, 2021;Ulrich & Miller, 2021). In comparison to these truncated designs, however, SPRTs are more efficient on average. Moreover, as SPRTs are based on likelihood ratios, sampling can be stopped and the test statistic (𝐿𝑅 𝑁 ) can be interpreted as a direct measure of statistical evidence at any point -unlike a 𝑝 value (Schnuerch & Erdfelder, 2020). Therefore, as long as 𝑁 max does not have to be known precisely in advance, SPRTs are a maximally efficient alternative to conventional fixed-sample procedures.

For the case of simple hypotheses, the SPRT has well-defined properties that may be described analytically (Wald, 1947). When extended to account for composite hypotheses, however, the exact properties cannot be determined analytically. While there has been a number of simulation studies recently investigating the properties of sequential 𝑡-tests, little is known about the sequential ANOVA's efficiency compared to the fixed-sample case, or about the test's sensitivity to violations of its underlying assumptions (e.g., Schnuerch & Erdfelder, 2020;Stefan et al., 2022). In this simulation study, we seek to fill this gap. In a first set of simulations, we investigate error rates and efficiency of the sequential ANOVA compared to the corresponding fixed ANOVA under ideal conditions, that is, when all assumptions underlying both tests are met. Subsequently, we look at how these properties are affected by imperfect conditions, namely, unequal group sizes and/or population variances, as well as violations of normality assumptions. Lastly, we also assess potential biases of effect size estimation following a sequential ANOVA. All simulation scripts, the simulation results and 1% of the simulated raw data can be found at the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/6yq5f/).

div.head: Settings of the Simulation
div.p: In every iteration of the simulation, we randomly drew 4 population data sets (𝑁 1 = 𝑁 2 = 𝑁 3 = 𝑁 4 = 20,000) with a certain effect structure from normal distributions to simulate a study with 4 independent groups. The population variances (𝜎 2 𝑖 ) were specified as 1. To vary the population means (𝜇 𝑖 ), we drew 4 raw means (𝑚 𝑖 ) from a standard normal distribution. These raw means were then transformed to match a specified effect size of Cohen's 𝑓 (𝑓 𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒 ) for 𝑘 = 4 groups. In the transformation, the raw means were z-standardized, scaled by 𝑓 𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒 , and corrected by √ 𝑘 𝑘-1 :

div.p: Then, we calculated a sequential and a fixed one-way ANOVA on samples from these simulated populations. The sequential ANOVA started with 2 data points in every group (i.e., 𝑘 × 2 = 8 data points in total), and one data point per group was added in every sequential step. The sequential data collection process was terminated as soon as the upper or lower threshold value for 𝐿𝑅 𝑛 was reached and a decision for one of the two hypotheses (𝐻 0 or 𝐻 1 ) was made. In contrast, the fixed ANOVA was performed on a sample with a fixed size that was determined by an a priori power analysis. We used an 𝛼 and 𝛽 level of .05 for the power analysis and the specification of the sequential ANOVA.

Altogether, 12 combinations of true and expected effect sizes were simulated (𝑓 𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒 = {0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.4}, 𝑓 𝑒𝑥𝑝 = {0.1, 0.25, 0.4}). Each combination was repeated 10,000 times (𝑁 𝑟 ). Thus, our results are based on 120,000 simulated cases. These are the simulation settings for our main simulation, which we will reference later.
We used seeds for all simulations and stored 1% of the raw data. The seed for an iteration is the sum of a hyper seed (we used 10,000) and the number of the iteration.

Therefore it was possible to get reproducible results while using parallelization to speed up the run time. All results were conducted multiple times with different seeds and the choice of seeds did not affect the pattern of results in a meaningful way.

div.head: Error Rates
div.p: Table 1 shows the simulated error rates of the sequential and the fixed ANOVA. To account for sampling error in the estimated rates, we calculated a 90% Clopper-Pearson interval as a criterion for inflated error rates. If the lower bound of the interval was equal to or larger than .05, the error rate was considered inflated. As expected, the sequential ANOVA controls the 𝛼 and 𝛽 error rates as long as the expected effect size is smaller than or equal to the true effect size in the population. Only if the true effect in the data is smaller than expected, the 𝛽 error rates exceed the nominal value. To understand the increasing 𝛽 error rates better, we investigated the error rates of a small effect (𝑓 𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒 = 0.10) while we slightly increased (+ 0.01) the expected effect size, starting from a perfect specification to a medium effect size (𝑓 𝑒𝑥𝑝 = {0.10, 0.11, 0.12..., 0.25}).
Unsurprisingly, the results highlight that even a small overestimation of the true effect size negatively impacts Type-II error rates, for sequential and fixed ANOVAs alike (see Figure 1).

the fixed-sample procedure in 87% of the cases. On average, the sequential ANOVA required 58% smaller samples than the conventional ANOVA. In the following, we will refer to this reduction in the required sample size as sample size efficiency. To summarize, the sequential ANOVA is overall clearly more efficient than the fixed ANOVA. The exact sample size efficiency depends on the effect size, however (see Table 2): The smaller the effect size, the higher the sample size efficiency of a sequential compared to a fixed-sample ANOVA. To better understand this pattern, it is helpful to look at the average sequential sample sizes necessary to reach a decision compared to the fixed sample sizes. This comparison can be seen in Table 3. Especially the combination of 𝑓 𝑒𝑥𝑝 = 0.10 and 𝑓 𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑒 = 0.40, where the true effect in the data was larger than expected, shows a striking difference in sample sizes. While the sample size of a sequential procedure is influenced by both, the expected effect size and the true effect size underlying the observed data, the sample size of a fixed design is solely based on the expected effect size. div.head: Simulations of Imperfect Conditions
div.p: Examining statistical procedures under ideal conditions is a necessary step to understand the test properties. However, since empirical research is rarely conducted under ideal circumstances, it is essential to study the properties of sequential ANOVAs in scenarios where certain assumptions are violated. We examined 4 scenarios in more detail:

(1) unequal group sample sizes, (2) unequal variances across groups, (3) unequal group sample sizes and variances, (4) and non-normally distributed data. This selection of scenarios is based on common scenarios of robustness analysis of sequential t-tests and fixed ANOVAs (Blanca et al., 2018;Glass et al., 1972;Lee & Fung, 1980;Lix et al., 1996;Schnuerch & Erdfelder, 2020).

div.head: Settings of the Simulation
div.p: In every iteration of the simulation, we randomly drew 4 population data sets with equal (𝑁 1 = 𝑁 2 = 𝑁 3 = 𝑁 4 = 20,000) or unequal (𝑁 1 = 𝑁 2 ≠ 𝑁 3 = 𝑁 4 ) group sample sizes, with a total sample size of 𝑁 = 80, 000 and with a certain effect structure from normal distributions to simulate a study with 4 independent groups. The ratios between the samples were chosen as (1,1,1,1), (1,1,2,2), and (2,2,1,1), meaning that in the unbalanced cases, the two largest groups had twice the amount of data at each sequential step than the two smallest groups.

Table 4 displays the cases where either the variance or the sample sizes in the groups vary, while Table 5 shows the cases where both variance and sample size differ between groups. If only the sample size ratio was unbalanced, the empirical 𝛽 was increased by a maximum of 2.3 percentage points (see Table 4). If only the variance was unbalanced between groups, the empirical 𝛼 was increased by a maximum of 2.5 percentage points.

When both the sample ratio and population variances were unbalanced, two scenarios could be distinguished: The population variance could be larger in groups with larger sample sizes, or it could be larger in groups with smaller sample sizes. As the first case may lead to an overall overestimation of the within-groups variance and, thus, an underestimation of the effect size, we did not observe an increase in error rates in this case.

In the second case, however, the effect size is overestimated due to an underestimated within-groups variance. Consequently, error rates were inflated in this case. Specifically, we observed an increase in 𝛼 by a maximum of 13 percentage points and an increase in 𝛽 by a maximum of 3.4 percentage points, see Table 5.

Overall, the sequential and the fixed ANOVA showed similar error rates when assumptions about group sizes and homoscedasticity were violated. However, the sequential ANOVA was still more efficient than the fixed-sample procedure. The mean sequential sample sizes required by the sequential procedure were consistently lower than the corresponding fixed sample sizes.

div.head: Estimation of Effect Sizes
div.p: SPRTs were developed to increase the efficiency of statistical decision-making while controlling error rates. However, even though hypothesis testing is the main focus in many applications, researchers are typically interested in effect size estimation following the hypothesis test (Fritz et al., 2012;Lovakov & Agadullina, 2021). Thus, discussing the limitations of effect size estimation in the context of a sequential ANOVA is relevant.

Let us assume that researchers want to estimate Cohen's 𝑓 from a sample that they collected using a sequential ANOVA and that they stopped the data collection process as soon as a decision was reached. Like in a fixed-sample setting, one could calculate Cohen's 𝑓 and a 95% Confidence Interval (CI). However, several issues should be considered.
First, Cohen's 𝑓 is known to be a biased estimate in fixed-sample applications (Lakens, 2013;Maxwell et al., 2017). Thus, a better estimate is given by (Maxwell et al., 2017, p. 150):

div.p: Second, the high sample size efficiency of sequential ANOVAs leads to smaller sample sizes on average. As is well known, smaller sample sizes are generally less precise in estimating population parameters than larger samples (Gigerenzer, 1989). Thus, there is a trade-off between a high sample size efficiency (leading to smaller samples on average) and estimation precision (requiring larger samples).

In addition, the use of sequential stopping rules produces biased estimates depending on the sample size. This phenomenon is not only known in the context of SPRTs but sequential procedures in general, such as group sequential designs (Pocock & Hughes, 1989) and the Sequential Bayes Factor Test (Schönbrodt et al., 2017). Figure 3 shows the link between the sample size and the estimated effect size in our simulations for different scenarios. Panel A shows the case of a large population effect size (𝑓 true = 0.40).

For small sample sizes and correct decisions (i.e., 𝐻 0 rejected), the estimates show an upward bias. The expected effect size also influenced the bias: The larger 𝑓 𝑒𝑥𝑝 , the larger the bias. For larger samples and correct rejections of 𝐻 0 , in contrast, the effect size was underestimated. The same pattern emerged when 𝐻 0 was incorrectly maintained: In this case, the effect was generally underestimated.

Panel B shows the case where there is no effect in the population. Here, overestimation of the effect size occured particularly when the expected effect was large or medium; thus, when sample sizes were rather small. Overall, these results indicate that small samples tend to overestimate the true effect size and large samples rather underestimate the true effect size.

From a meta-analytic viewpoint, however, this bias is not generally problematic. A meta-analytic weighted average of estimated effect sizes across all simulated samples (using fadjusted ) was essentially unbiased (s. Table A1 in the Appendix for more information).
This finding replicates results from Schönbrodt et al. (2017), who showed similar results for meta-analytic effect size estimation using the SBFT.

Finally, a good strategy to calculate confidence intervals for effect size estimates following a sequential test is an ongoing topic of discussion (Bhattacharjee & Mukhopadhyay, 2015;Ulrich & Miller, 2021). A naive approach would use the same calculation method that is used for fixed samples; however, the coverage rate of these confidence intervals is typically lower than the nominal value. Across simulation conditions, we found that the 95% CI calculated for the effect sizes estimated from our simulated sequential samples covered the population effect size in 93% of the cases. Thus, if unbiased effect size estimation is the primary aim of the study, a sequential testing approach may not be the optimal choice.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: In this paper, we presented a sequential ANOVA based on Abraham Wald's (1945) SPRT to increase the efficiency of statistical decision making and demonstrated its usefulness in a series of simulation studies. The SPRT is based on the nominal standard for hypothesis testing in psychology, namely, the Neyman-Pearson framework (1933), and it was designed to control decision errors in a maximally efficient way. It uses a likelihood ratio (𝐿𝑅) as a test statistic which indicates the relative evidence for one over a competing hypothesis. 𝐿𝑅𝑠 have the advantage that they are easily interpretable (e.g., 𝐿𝑅 = 20 means that the data are 20 times more likely under one hypothesis than under the other hypothesis) and they can be used to quantify evidence for the null as well as for the alternative hypothesis. In addition, SPRTs exert full control over 𝛼 and 𝛽 error rates and can be applied to any testing situation as long as the 𝐿𝑅 is fully specified.

Although SPRTs have many benefits and have existed in the statistics literature for nearly 80 years, they are not widely known and rarely considered part of the methodological toolbox of psychological researchers. We argue that SPRTs can be a powerful and efficient alternative to fixed sample designs and a major asset in overcoming the problem of underpowered studies (Button et al., 2013;Rossi, 1990;Szucs & Ioannidis, 2017). Especially research with limited resources, such as neuromiaging research where studies are often costly in terms of monetary and time resources, can benefit from the high efficiency of SPRTs. The SPRT also caters to moral considerations: A clinical study, for example, where participants in a control group may receive an inferior treatment, has an ethical obligation to use as few participants as possible, that is, make use of the most efficient statistical procedure. Moreover, as the SPRT represents a balanced decision-making process between two hypotheses, its application increases the chance that null effects (i.e., decisions in favor of 𝐻 0 ) are published, thus helping to reduce the notorious file drawer problem (Rosenthal, 1979). To enhance hypothesis testing efficiency in the mentioned cases, we implemented a sequential ANOVA based on the SPRT in the R package sprtt. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of its properties, comparing them directly to a fixed-sample ANOVA.

div.head: Simulation Results
div.p: In our main simulation study, we showed that in most of the simulated cases, the sequential sample sizes were smaller than the fixed sample sizes: On average, less than half of the data needed to be collected using a sequential instead of a fixed ANOVA. The sequential ANOVA is especially efficient if the expected effect size is small, allowing for a more conservative and realistic specification of the expected effect size.

Robustness analyses showed similar properties between the sequential and the fixed ANOVA in terms of error probability control, while the sequential test was consistently more efficient than the conventional test even when basic assumptions of the tests were violated. Our results replicate other simulation studies that investigated the robustness of sequential t-tests (Lee & Fung, 1980;Schnuerch & Erdfelder, 2020) or fixed ANOVAs (Lix et al., 1996;Schmider et al., 2010), further supporting the notion that sequential tests provide a useful alternative to conventional test procedures.

div.head: Limitations of Sequential ANOVAs
div.p: Despite their favorable properties, we do not promote sequential ANOVAs as the optimal choice under all circumstances. The selection of an appropriate testing procedure requires researchers to weigh the benefits and limitations of various options in their statistical toolbox and carefully choose the option that best fits the problem at hand (Gigerenzer, 2004). The first limitation of SPRTs is that the exact sample size is not known beforehand. When planning a study, one could use information about average sample sizes from simulations to get an idea of the required sample size. However, if the exact sample size must be known beforehand, there are better choices than the SPRT, such as fixed-sample designs or other, truncated sequential tests (e.g., Miller & Ulrich, 2021;Pramanik et al., 2021;Proschan et al., 2006).

Even though the SPRT will terminate with a finite sample size (Wald, 1947), it is not guaranteed that it terminates before the available resources are exhausted. Thus, theoretically, it could happen that data collection has to be stopped before a decision has been reached. In this case, researchers must refrain from making a decision as error rates

will not be controlled for this altered procedure. However, there is no reason not to interpret the available statistical evidence provided by the 𝐿𝑅 at that point (Schnuerch et al., 2022;Schnuerch & Erdfelder, 2020). A possible strategy is thus to specify a maximum sample size for the sequential ANOVA (𝑁 max ) based on the a priori sample size of the power analysis for a corresponding fixed design. If sampling terminates before reaching 𝑁 max , a decision can be made accordingly. If 𝑁 max is reached before a decision threshold is crossed, in contrast, researchers can stop and report the evidence provided by the 𝐿𝑅 without making a finite statistical decision. Our simulations showed that the risk is low, however: Across simulation conditions, the sequential procedure terminated in about 90%
of the cases before reaching the sample size of the corresponding fixed-sample test.

Another limitation is that effect size estimation following a sequential test may be biased. Small sequential samples tend to overestimate the population effect, and large sequential samples tend to underestimate the population effect. From a meta-analytic perspective that takes into account both early and late terminations at either decision threshold, however, these biases balance each other out (see Schönbrodt et al., 2017).
Nevertheless, if the primary goal of a study is to estimate a population effect size as precisely as possible, a sequential testing procedure (of any kind) cannot be recommended.
In contrast, if the main goal is to test a statistical hypothesis -is there an effect of interest or not? -a sequential ANOVA is a valid and highly efficient tool.

Consequently, another limitation concerns the calculation of the confidence interval (CI). The naive approach -using the calculation method for fixed samples (Steiger, 2004) results in a CI that does not include the true effect sizes as often as it should (Ulrich & Miller, 2021). Using a non-parametric calculation procedure like bootstrapping showed even worse results in the simulation study of Bhattacharjee and Mukhopadhyay (2015).
Although the naive approach is flawed, the calculation of the naive CI could still be helpful to some researchers to understand effect size estimates of small sequential samples better.
Further research is needed to improve the calculation method for CIs in this context.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The sequential ANOVA based on the SPRT proposed herein is an efficient alternative to classical fixed-sample ANOVAs. It exerts strict control of 𝛼 and 𝛽 error rates and requires on average around 50% smaller samples than conventional test procedures.

This advantage in sample size efficiency remains even when underlying assumptions are violated, in which case the sequential ANOVA is similarly robust as the fixed-sample ANOVA. By implementing the sequential ANOVA in the user-friendly R package sprtt and thoroughly investigating its properties in a range of possible scenarios by means of simulations, we hope to make the sequential procedure more accessible and pave its way into the statistics toolbox of psychological researchers in all subfields.
